title: Count Subsets by Sum

statement.md: A risk engine counts the number of ways to pick a subset of trades whose notional sums to exactly a target — the combinatorial core of exposure bucketing. Given $n$ values and a target, count subsets (including possibly the empty one) whose elements sum to the target, modulo $10^9+7$.

inputFormat: First line: $n$ and $target$ ($1 \le n \le 200$, $0 \le target \le 20{,}000$). Second line: $n$ positive integers $a_i$ ($1 \le a_i \le target$).
outputFormat: The number of subsets summing to $target$, modulo $10^9 + 7$.
hints: dp[s] = number of subsets seen so far with sum s; process items one at a time.
Iterate sums DOWNWARD so each item is used at most once (0/1 knapsack direction).

editorial.md: Classic 0/1 knapsack counting. State: after processing the first $i$ items, $dp[s]$ = number of subsets with sum $s$. Transition per item $v$: $dp[s] += dp[s-v]$, iterated for $s$ from $target$ down to $v$ — downward so the $dp[s-v]$ being read is from the *previous* item's row (each item used once). The answer is $dp[target] \bmod 10^9+7$.

The modulus is there because counts grow exponentially (200 ones summing to 200 has $\binom{200}{200}$-style magnitude). The empty subset is naturally counted by $dp[0]=1$: with target 0 the answer is 1, which the test set checks. Complexity $O(n \cdot target)$ = 4M operations worst case.

solutions.python:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0]); target = int(data[1])
vals = [int(x) for x in data[2:2+n]]
dp = [0]*(target+1)
dp[0] = 1
for v in vals:
    for s in range(target, v-1, -1):
        dp[s] += dp[s-v]
print(dp[target] % 1000000007)
